worked_example.title: Screening test — Bayes update
worked_example.problem_statement: A disease has prevalence P(D) = 0.01. A test has sensitivity P(+|D) = 0.95 and false-positive rate P(+|not D) = 0.10. A randomly selected person tests positive. Find P(D|+).
worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Before uncovering each solution step, write the next quantity you need and why.

steps.label: Compute the evidence P(+)
steps.attempt_cue: Write P(+) = P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|not D)P(not D) and substitute the given values.
steps.explanation: Law of total probability expands the positive-test rate across disease and no-disease paths.

steps.label: Compute the posterior P(D|+)
steps.explanation: Posterior equals prior × likelihood, normalised by the evidence from Step 1.

worked_example.final_answer: P(+) = 0.1085; P(D|+) ≈ 0.0876. Refuse equating P(D|+) with P(+|D) = 0.95.
worked_example.common_pitfall: Taking P(D|+) = 0.95 (sensitivity) ignores the base rate and the large contribution of false positives to P(+).

knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 5.1.1
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly states Bayes' theorem for a simple conditional probability update?
knowledge_checks.body: Select the Bayes update with prior, likelihood, and evidence.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Bayes combines prior, likelihood, and evidence. Equating P(A|B) with P(B|A) or dropping the base rate reverses or omits required pieces.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Equating posterior with likelihood or ignoring the base rate.

choices.label: Bayes' theorem updates P(A|B) from P(B|A), P(A), and P(B): posterior equals prior times likelihood divided by evidence. A simple update requires all three pieces, not confusing posterior with likelihood alone.
P(A|B) always equals P(B|A) because conditioning is symmetric for any events A and B.
Bayes' theorem means posterior equals likelihood; the base rate P(A) never enters a positive-test update.
Updating a conditional requires only the prior P(A); likelihood and normalising evidence are optional labels.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 5.1.1
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Screening: P(D) = 0.01, P(+|D) = 0.95, P(+|not D) = 0.10. A case tests positive. Which statement is correct?
knowledge_checks.body: Compute P(D|+) via Bayes; refuse P(D|+) = P(+|D).
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Evidence P(+) = 0.1085 and posterior ≈ 0.0876. Sensitivity 0.95 is not the posterior. Prior alone or the false-positive rate alone is wrong.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: P(+)=0.1085; P(D|+)≈0.0876; refuse posterior equals likelihood.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Taking P(D|+) = 0.95 or ignoring base-rate normalisation.

choices.label: P(+) = 0.95×0.01 + 0.10×0.99 = 0.1085. P(D|+) = 0.0095/0.1085 ≈ 0.0876. Equating P(D|+) with P(+|D) = 0.95 ignores the base rate; Bayes multiplies prior by likelihood and normalises.
P(D|+) = P(+|D) = 0.95 because the test is accurate when disease is present, so the positive predictive value equals the sensitivity.
P(D|+) = 0.01 because the prior prevalence is the answer once a case tests positive.
P(D|+) = 0.10 because P(+|not D) = 0.10 dominates the update for any positive screen.
